messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Minh was eighteen when the typhoon hit his family’s coastal town in Vietnam. The water rose faster than anyone expected; by the time they tried to flee, it was waist-deep and black with debris. He remembers being pinned against a collapsed wall, his neck twisted at an angle as he gasped for air. Mud and saltwater forced their way into his mouth, and even now, four years later, the taste can return without warning—a metallic, gritty film on his tongue that feels as real as the day it happened. He survived, but the house was destroyed and two neighbors drowned. Minh made it to America shortly after for college, leaving behind a community that had unraveled in the storm’s wake.

Now twenty-two and working as a UX designer in a downtown office, Minh notices his neck stiffens after hours of hunching over wireframes. A dull ache starts at his shoulders and climbs to the base of his skull. That physical sensation—something as ordinary as sitting too long—can suddenly pull him back: he feels the water around him, hears the wood groaning, and the whole scene rushes in with a clarity that makes no sense. The memory itself feels unreal, too extreme to have actually happened to him, yet his body reacts as if it is happening now. Sometimes the emotional intensity rises without any image at all—a wave of terror or helplessness that floods him while he’s staring at a screen, leaving him breathless and unable to explain why. Those episodes often leave him feeling physically ill, nauseated and shaky for the rest of the day. In the hours that follow, he finds himself scrutinizing his coworkers’ smiles more harshly, certain their pleasantries hide the same indifference he saw from neighbors after the storm.

Minh has come to believe that people are not what they seem. Back in the village, neighbors who had appeared generous looked the other way when his family needed help lifting debris. In the office, coworkers smile and ask about his weekend, but he is certain their kindness is a mask. He feels set apart, isolated by an experience they could never understand, and he no longer belongs anywhere—not in the United States, where he passes for a quiet immigrant, and not in his hometown, which is now a different place. These appraisals tighten his vigilance: every minor ache, every wave of nausea becomes a warning sign that something bad is about to happen, and he scans his body constantly for signs of danger. The neck pain comes more often now, in part because he hunches harder when he is anxious, and each twinge feeds the cycle.

When the memory surfaces unbidden, it deepens his sense of alienation. If the event feels unreal to him, how could anyone else believe it? He stops himself from speaking about it at work, and the silence widens the distance. The more the memory intrudes, the more his neck aches in anticipation—each recollection seems to sharpen his body’s sensitivity to the slightest tension, turning ordinary stiffness into a fresh alert. Last month, during a team stand-up, someone mentioned a storm delay on the news. Minh’s neck seized, he tasted mud, and he excused himself to the bathroom, where he stood gripping the sink until his hands stopped shaking. After that, he began arriving late and leaving early to avoid casual conversations where disaster topics might arise. His manager noticed his withdrawal; a project lead asked if everything was okay. Minh said nothing.

What finally brought him to seek help was a morning when he woke with the taste already in his mouth, his neck locked, and the feeling that he was drowning in plain air. He called a therapist’s office that same afternoon. He is not sure anyone can truly understand, but he is tired of living inside the loop—the ache, the memory, the distrust, the ache again. More than anything, he wants to feel as though he belongs somewhere, even if he no longer knows where that is.
